extracted.intended_audience: state policymakers (governors, legislators), state agency officials, child support enforcement agencies, and community fatherhood program leaders
extracted.subtask_description: Policy and program guidance for state governments and agencies to redesign child support, tax, outreach, and service-delivery policies to better support low-income non-custodial fathers and responsible fatherhood programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pass-throughs
rubrics_metrics.description: Reinstate their state's child support pass-throughs or strengthen existing pass-throughs to allow at least some of the child support paid by low-income fathers to be paid directly to their families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States have discretion under current law to pass through more support to families. Examples: Wisconsin enacted a 100 percent pass-through and disregards child support when calculating W-2 eligibility; Connecticut and Vermont have also tried full pass-throughs. Pass-throughs can speed welfare exit and increase family income; consider federal waiver/funding implications and whether to disregard support in benefit eligibility calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspend/reduce/forgive TANF-related state child support debt for program participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors and legislators should forgive or decrease TANF-related child support debt for fathers who participate in programs designed to increase their earnings and improve their parenting skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States can suspend, reduce, or forgive child support debts that are owed to the state (not to the family). For instance, waive TANF-related debts for fathers who participate in employment and fatherhood programs and subsequently maintain up-to-date child support payments. Debt forgiveness gives cooperative fathers an opportunity to start anew; fathers would still owe families arrears that accumulate before or after leaving TANF. Examples: Washington forgives state debt for non-custodial parents who reunite and prove hardship; Vermont suspends payments when parents reunite and combined income is below 225% FPL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedicate TANF-related child support revenues to fatherhood programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors and legislators should dedicate revenues from TANF-related child support collections to fund responsible fatherhood programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a portion of state-collected TANF-related support to underwrite job-training, fatherhood programming, seed grants, and other direct services aimed at increasing fathers' employment and parenting capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-support reserves in child support guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors and legislators should rewrite state child support guidelines to allow self-support reserves for non-custodial working parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A self-support reserve allows non-custodial parents to keep a portion of their income to live on regardless of obligations, protecting low-income working fathers from overwhelming demands. Examples: New York law permits reductions as low as $25/month and caps child support debt for low-income non-custodial parents at $500. Implement clear rules for when judges may reduce orders based on ability to pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amend state Earned Income Tax Credits (EITC) to benefit fathers who pay support
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors and legislators should amend their state Earned Income Tax Credits to give fathers credit for the child support they pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three suggested approaches from the Urban Institute: (1) Allow non-custodial parents who meet support obligations and the EITC income criteria to claim the same EITC benefit claimed by families with children (cap at amount of support paid). (2) Give custodial parents priority for the EITC but allow non-custodial parents to claim it if custodial parents are ineligible due to high income. (3) Give non-custodial parents who pay child support half of the tax credit amount they would receive if the child lived with them, or the amount of child support paid, whichever is lower. These changes would incentivize paying support and increase fathers’ take-home earnings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include contest/modification/visitation contact in enforcement notices
rubrics_metrics.description: In every notice they mail out, child support enforcement offices should include a telephone number fathers can call if they want to contest paternity, seek modification of a child support order, or negotiate custody and visitation issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing an explicit contact lowers procedural barriers and encourages fathers to engage constructively instead of avoiding enforcement notices; include clear instructions and referral options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspend/forgive state child support debt when parents reunite or marry
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors and legislators should suspend or forgive child support debt owned to the state when parents reunite or marry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States can condition suspension/forgiveness on reunification or marriage and potentially on combined income thresholds (e.g., Vermont suspends payments when parents reunite and have combined incomes below 225% FPL). This policy can encourage family reunification and reduce barriers to fathers' economic participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appoint Fatherhood Commissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors should appoint Fatherhood Commissions to advise policymakers on how state agencies can better serve fathers and families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commissions provide ongoing cross-agency advice, help coordinate initiatives, and can include representatives from nonprofits, business, judiciary, and community leaders to recommend policy and program changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiate and fund public awareness campaigns promoting responsible fatherhood
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors and legislators should initiate and fund public awareness campaigns that promote responsible fatherhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage resources such as the National Fatherhood Initiative (NFI) which has produced radio/TV ads and materials; secure donated airtime and tailor messages to target audiences (e.g., use ordinary father images rather than celebrities when appropriate). Examples include billboard campaigns with sports teams and Spanish-language materials. Campaigns should aim to change public attitudes and fathers' own attitudes about involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide funding and technical assistance for father resource centers
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors and legislators should provide funding and technical assistance to community-based organizations that develop father resource centers to serve as local clearinghouses for training and advice to fathers and social service agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resource centers can centralize training, referrals (job training, legal help), materials, and evaluation tools for local fatherhood programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct agency audits for father-friendliness
rubrics_metrics.description: All state agencies should conduct agency audits for father-friendliness to assess how they can expand and improve services to fathers and to determine whether they can eliminate bureaucratic barriers that discourage men from supporting their children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audits examine policies/procedures (e.g., forms, eligibility rules, outreach practices) and recommend changes such as simplifying access, creating father-focused points of contact, and removing punitive practices that undermine employment or involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a fathers’ component in diversity training
rubrics_metrics.description: All state agencies should include a fathers’ component in any diversity training that their employees are required to attend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training modules should cover barriers faced by low-income fathers, resources available in the community, and how front-line staff can engage fathers as resources to families rather than assuming unwillingness to pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visit programs, convene hearings, and invite fathers to speak
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors, legislators, and agency officials should all visit a few fatherhood programs. Elected officials also should convene fatherhood hearings or town hall meetings and invite low-income non-custodial fathers to speak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct exposure helps policymakers understand program operations, service gaps, and fathers’ perspectives; hearings facilitate public input and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build grassroots support and community forums
rubrics_metrics.description: Policymakers and organizations should mobilize local leaders and build grassroots support through community forums to promote responsible fatherhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NFI has helped community forums and provided materials; grassroots work includes mobilizing civic groups, faith communities, and businesses to change local attitudes and support program development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen to fathers and inventory local programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Take the time to learn what already exists in the community — visiting programs, talking to fathers, inviting them to speak at community forums — to identify service gaps and barriers local fathers face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct an inventory of local programs (the National Practitioners’ Network estimates nearly 1,000 programs), solicit direct feedback from fathers, and use that input to design or adapt services rather than imposing top-down solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign trained staff and add fragile-families training modules
rubrics_metrics.description: Child support and TANF offices should assign trained staff to handle cases where the father is a participant in fatherhood programs and add a module about fragile families to training curricula for new caseworkers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training should include information about low-income fathers, common barriers, community resources, and how to support fathers' involvement; dedicated staff signals commitment and improves case handling for program participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt father-friendly agency practices (outreach, volunteering, unit creation)
rubrics_metrics.description: State agencies should make commitments to think of fathers as an integral part of the family and ensure their policies are father-friendly (e.g., require TANF caseworkers to provide outreach to fathers, encourage fathers to volunteer in Head Start, create fatherhood units).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hennepin County assigned staff to the FATHER Project and changed internal practices. Agency-level changes can include outreach efforts, program referrals, reinstating drivers' licenses where appropriate, and creating father-focused services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seed grants and small grant funding for community programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide small grants to start and sustain community-based fatherhood programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seed grants help programs launch; examples: Virginia Fatherhood Campaign awards up to $25,000 seed grants; Florida commission awards small grants (maximum $50,000). Combine seed funding with technical assistance and evaluation support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program evaluation and outcome measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach communities how to evaluate outcomes of fatherhood programs and build evaluation into program design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage rigorous evaluations (e.g., tracking welfare exit, employment, visitation, child well-being), use evaluations to refine programs, and seek partnerships with research institutions for formal assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partnerships and referrals rather than trying to be all things
rubrics_metrics.description: Fatherhood programs should form partnerships and refer fathers to other services (job training, placement) rather than attempting to provide every service in-house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: VFC-funded programs typically refer job training and placement services; partnerships with workforce agencies, community colleges, and nonprofits increase reach and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted messaging and culturally appropriate materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Design public-awareness and program materials tailored to specific audiences (e.g., Spanish-language brochures, barbershop campaigns, ordinary fathers in ads rather than celebrities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use audience testing/focus groups to shape messages (Virginia VFC shifted from celebrities to ordinary fathers after focus groups). Place materials where target men frequent (barbershops, sporting events) and tailor images and language to cultural groups.
